themes.label: The hardness proofs
themes.description: The two 1998 proofs that two-letter HP folding is NP-complete.

themes.label: Folding variants
themes.description: Hardness with another alphabet, energy, lattice or angle rule, a given region, or a restricted set of folds.

themes.label: Source problems and gadgets
themes.description: Problems a reduction can start from, and constructions the proofs borrow.

themes.label: Approximation
themes.description: Algorithms that reach a fixed fraction of the optimal score.

themes.label: Other lattices: contact bounds and exact search
themes.description: How many contacts H's can make on the face-centred cubic lattice, and how far exact search reaches there. None of these papers proves hardness.

themes.label: Inverse folding and sequence design
themes.description: Given a shape, choose the H/P string. One published hardness proof in this area is wrong.

themes.label: Formalization
themes.description: The HP model in Lean, and NP-completeness in Lean, Coq and Isabelle.

themes.label: Surveys and background
themes.description: The origin of the model, surveys and lectures that restate the proofs, and a classical inequality.

papers.title: An inequality related to the isoperimetric inequality
papers.gist: Bounds the size of a set by the sizes of its projections onto the coordinate planes.
papers.takeaway: Theorem 2 is the discrete form: for a set S of unit cubes, |S|² is at most the product of the sizes of its three projections. The paper has no case of equality.
papers.why: Berger and Leighton's cube lemma says that n³ H's have the most contacts exactly when they fill a cube. They give no source. Its inequality is this one; the case of equality is proved by Atkins and Hart.

papers.title: Complexity Results for Multiprocessor Scheduling under Resource Constraints
papers.gist: A scheduling result that is the first hardness proof for 3-PARTITION.
papers.takeaway: The paper never names 3-PARTITION. Its Theorem 3.5 is 3-PARTITION without the size bounds, stated for scheduling. Section 4 notes that the numbers in the proof stay polynomially bounded, so the hardness is strong.
papers.why: The original source when the sizes in a reduction become lengths.

papers.title: The Planar Hamiltonian Circuit Problem is NP-Complete
papers.gist: Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete in cubic, 3-connected planar graphs.
papers.why: Bounded degree and planarity make it easier to draw the graph in a lattice.

papers.title: Computers and Intractability: A Guide to the Theory of NP-Completeness
papers.gist: The standard catalogue of NP-complete problems. It proves 3-PARTITION strongly NP-complete.
papers.takeaway: Theorem 4.4 covers 3-PARTITION with sizes strictly between B/4 and B/2. The book's bin packing asks for bins filled to at most the capacity. Berger and Leighton modify it to exact filling with even sizes.
papers.why: Strong NP-completeness matters here. Item sizes become lengths in the string, so the numbers have to be written in unary.

relations.note: Proves 3-PARTITION strongly NP-complete (Theorem 4.4) and credits the 1975 paper, which proved a form without the size bounds.

papers.title: The NP-completeness of the Hamiltonian cycle problem in planar digraphs with degree bound two
papers.gist: Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete in directed planar graphs of degree at most 3.
papers.why: The first link in the chain of reductions that ends at Hamiltonicity in grid graphs.

papers.title: Hamilton Paths in Grid Graphs
papers.gist: Hamiltonian path and cycle are NP-complete in grid graphs.
papers.takeaway: In rectangular grid graphs, Hamiltonian paths between two given vertices are decided in polynomial time.
papers.why: A source problem without numbers. A Hamiltonian path of a grid graph is a self-avoiding walk that fills a region exactly. We found no reduction from it to HP folding.

relations.note: Lemma 2.1 starts from Hamiltonicity of planar digraphs of low degree.

papers.title: Planar Formulae and Their Uses
papers.gist: Planar 3SAT is NP-complete.
papers.why: Planar SAT lets gadgets be laid out in the plane. Paterson and Przytycka use it for 2D string folding.

papers.title: On Two Geometric Problems Related to the Travelling Salesman Problem
papers.gist: Hamiltonian path stays NP-complete in grid graphs of maximum degree 3.
papers.takeaway: Theorem 2. The paper states no cycle version with this degree bound.
papers.why: With degree at most 3, every vertex keeps a free lattice side, room for a P (our remark). The paper uses that side in its Theorem 3.

relations.note: Hamiltonian path, restricted to grid graphs of maximum degree 3 (Theorem 2).

papers.title: Theory for the folding and stability of globular proteins
papers.gist: Introduces the HP model.
papers.takeaway: Hydrophobic residues drive folding by gathering in a compact core.
papers.why: The origin of the model that both hardness proofs study.
papers.statusNote: We know it through Berger and Leighton's references.

papers.title: Three-Dimensional Circuit Layouts
papers.gist: Layout of graphs in three-dimensional grids, with bounds on volume and wire length.
papers.takeaway: Berger and Leighton cite it for general methods of 3D wire routing. They use no lemma from it; their routing lemmas are their own.
papers.why: The routing is the part of Berger and Leighton's proof that a simpler proof would most like to avoid.

papers.title: Computational complexity of a problem in molecular structure prediction
papers.gist: Folding a path on the diamond lattice under angle rules is NP-complete.
papers.takeaway: The reduction is from PARTITION. Runs of the chain encode the numbers, and the chain length is exponential in the size of the instance.
papers.why: Chain lengths encode numbers, as in Berger and Leighton. Here the numbers are in binary, so the hardness is only weak.

relations.note: Diamond-lattice paths with turn rules. Berger and Leighton note that it ignores compactness and has many parameters.

papers.title: Complexity of protein folding
papers.gist: Re-embedding a graph of charges at low energy is NP-complete, in 2D and 3D.
papers.takeaway: The given edge lengths of the graph must be kept, so the object folded is a graph, not a chain. The reduction is from 3-dimensional matching.
papers.why: It folds a graph instead of a string, which gives the reduction more control over the shape.

relations.note: Folds a graph of charged atoms instead of a string, as Berger and Leighton point out.

papers.title: Finding the lowest free energy conformation of a protein is an NP-hard problem: proof and implications
papers.gist: An early NP-hardness proof for a lattice model whose potential is part of the input.
papers.takeaway: The reduction is from optimal linear arrangement. The potential forces part of the chain onto a line. The authors could not prove hardness for an HP-like model on the square lattice.
papers.why: Hardness comes easily once the energy can pin down the geometry. The H/P energy cannot do that.

relations.note: A non-HP lattice model. Berger and Leighton list it as earlier work.

papers.title: Fast protein folding in the hydrophobic-hydrophilic model within three-eighths of optimal
papers.gist: Simple folding algorithms that reach 1/4 of the optimal score in 2D and 3/8 in 3D.
papers.takeaway: The ratios are asymptotic, and the algorithms run in linear or quadratic time. They rest on a parity bound: the lattices are bipartite, so an H can touch only H's at positions of the other parity. In 2D a fold has at most 2X + T contacts, where X counts the H's of the smaller parity class and T the ends of the string that are H's of that class. The paper lists the complexity of HP folding as open and conjectures that it is NP-hard.
papers.why: A fold meets the parity bound only if every free side of the smaller class touches an H. This is the 2D counterpart of Berger and Leighton's perfect fold.

papers.title: Invariant Patterns in Crystal Lattices: Implications for Protein Folding Algorithms
papers.gist: One recipe gives constant-factor folding algorithms on many lattices at once.
papers.takeaway: An approximation algorithm needs only a small pattern in the lattice: two rows that can face each other, and room for loops. Every lattice that contains the square-lattice pattern or the triangular one gets an algorithm within a constant factor of the best score. That covers the cubic, diamond, hexagonal and face-centred cubic lattices; only the diamond lattice gets an explicit ratio, 1/8.
papers.why: Approximation is settled up to constants on all the common lattices. The method maps folds of one lattice into another, so it carries algorithms across lattices but cannot carry NP-hardness.

relations.note: Generalizes its algorithm from the square and cubic lattices to every lattice that contains the same pattern.
Generalizes the triangular-lattice rules to lattices with triangles.
Cited for hardness on the cubic lattice.

papers.title: On the complexity of string folding
papers.gist: String folding with an unbounded alphabet is NP-complete in 2D and 3D.
papers.takeaway: Only identical letters bond. The 2D proof reduces from planar 3SAT, the 3D proof from 3SAT.
papers.why: The predecessor of both proofs. Its gadgets are rigid because only identical letters bond. Two letters cannot provide that.

relations.note: The 2D proof reduces from planar 3SAT. The 3D proof reduces from 3SAT.
Unbounded alphabet. The two-letter HP case was its open problem.
Its 3D proof uses the principle behind Berger and Leighton's perfect fold: a maximal score forces rigid gadgets.

papers.title: Local Rules for Protein Folding on a Triangular Lattice and Generalized Hydrophobicity in the HP Model
papers.gist: Simple folding rules reach 6/11 of the best score on the triangular lattice, and 3/5 in 3D.
papers.takeaway: The rules fold any string in linear time; the ratios hold for long strings. The 3D lattice is a stack of triangular layers in which every node has twelve neighbours, drawn as the face-centred cubic lattice. With no parity rule to lean on, the upper bound counts, for each H, the free sides lost where an H meets a P along the string.
papers.why: The source of the 6/11 ratio, still the best we know for the triangular lattice. The authors write that in 1997 nobody knew whether folding on the square or the triangular lattice is NP-hard. The square case was settled a year later; we found no hardness proof for the triangular one.

relations.note: The same kind of guarantee, moved from the square lattice to the triangular lattice.
Cited for hardness when the alphabet is unbounded.

papers.title: On the computational complexity of sequence design problems
papers.gist: Claims that canonical HP sequence design is NP-complete in 2D and 3D.
papers.takeaway: Berman et al. later showed that the 2D reduction is wrong.
papers.why: A published hardness proof in this area that did not hold.

papers.title: Lattice and Off-Lattice Side Chain Models of Protein Folding: Linear Time Structure Prediction Better than 86% of Optimal
papers.gist: With side chains on the face-centred cubic lattice, a linear-time fold reaches 31/36 of the best score.
papers.takeaway: In this model each residue is a bead hanging off an unlabelled backbone, so the H's can pack more tightly than in the plain model. The algorithm stacks the H beads in eight columns. On the cubic lattice the same idea gives 2/5.
papers.why: A different model, so its ratios say nothing direct about the plain chain on the face-centred cubic lattice. The paper proves no hardness.

relations.note: Reuses its folding point on the cubic lattice.
The face-centred cubic algorithm builds on the star folding of Agarwala et al.

papers.title: Robust proofs of NP-hardness for protein folding: general lattices and energy potentials
papers.gist: With an unbounded alphabet, folding is NP-complete on every finitely representable lattice.
papers.takeaway: Theorem 1 extends Unger and Moult's reduction from optimal linear arrangement. Theorem 2 proves hardness on the cubic lattice for a class of distance potentials, by reduction from Hamiltonian path. The paper does not mention the HP model, and it asks for hardness with contact energies and a finite alphabet.
papers.why: Hardness that survives a change of lattice. Nothing follows for the two-letter HP model.

relations.note: Theorem 1 extends Unger and Moult's result to every finitely representable lattice.
Discussed as related work. Berger and Leighton describe the paper as a generalization of it.

papers.title: When Hamming Meets Euclid: The Approximability of Geometric TSP and MST
papers.gist: Embeds a graph by codewords whose Hamming distance tells whether two vertices are adjacent.
papers.why: Crescenzi et al. use this embedding in the 2D proof.

papers.title: Hamiltonian Cycles in Solid Grid Graphs
papers.gist: Hamiltonian cycle is polynomial in solid grid graphs, those without holes.
papers.takeaway: The algorithm merges the cycles of a 2-factor. The paper says nothing about Hamiltonian paths.
papers.why: A reduction that encodes Hamiltonian cycle as filling a region therefore needs holes or obstacles (our remark).

relations.note: Settles an open question of Itai et al.: on grid graphs without holes, Hamiltonian cycle is polynomial.

papers.title: Protein Folding in the Hydrophobic-Hydrophilic (HP) Model is NP-Complete
papers.gist: HP folding on the cubic lattice is NP-complete, by reduction from bin packing.
papers.takeaway: The string is built so that a perfect fold puts its H's in a cube and its pieces into bins on one face. That a perfect fold gives a packing takes 1.5 pages of counting. Building the fold from a packing takes explicit coordinates and six routing lemmas. The journal version has the same proof as the conference version.
papers.why: The base paper of this project. Most of its length goes into the explicit fold and the routing of the linkers, the runs of P's that join the pieces.

relations.note: Reduces from an exact, even-size form of Garey and Johnson's bin packing. Its strong NP-completeness follows from 3-PARTITION.
The cube lemma (Fact 3.1) is cited as a classic result without a source. Its inequality is Theorem 2 of Loomis and Whitney; the equality case is not in that paper.
Cited for general methods of 3D wire routing. The routing lemmas (3.3–3.8) are Berger and Leighton's own.
Studies the HP model, which the paper credits to Dill.
Hart and Istrail had listed the complexity of HP folding as open and conjectured NP-hardness.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Protein Folding
papers.gist: HP folding on the square lattice is NP-complete, by reduction from Hamiltonian path.
papers.takeaway: A Hadamard code makes every non-edge of the graph cost extra losses. The proof that a fold within the loss budget gives a Hamiltonian path takes 11 pages of the journal version and 25 pages of appendices. A 3D version is sketched in one paragraph.
papers.why: The only proof for the square lattice. Its target is a budget of losses instead of a perfect fold.

relations.note: Trevisan's Hadamard-code embedding turns non-adjacent vertices into extra losses.
The same question on the square lattice, proved independently. The paper credits Berger and Leighton with the 3D case.
Hart and Istrail had listed the complexity of HP folding as open and conjectured NP-hardness.

papers.title: Spatial codes and the hardness of string folding problems
papers.gist: With about 10³⁰⁰ letters, string folding is NP-hard and MAX SNP-hard.
papers.takeaway: On the cubic lattice, under randomized reductions. Each letter becomes a random codeword (a spatial code). Hardness of approximation for HP folding is left open.
papers.why: Shows how far generic methods go. The authors write that two letters would need a new idea.

relations.note: The single-string result adapts Paterson and Przytycka's 3D reduction so that it preserves gaps.
A finite alphabet of about 10³⁰⁰ letters on the cubic lattice.

papers.title: On the intractability of protein folding with a finite alphabet of amino acids
papers.gist: Folding with 12 letters on the cubic lattice is NP-complete.
papers.takeaway: The contact energies form a designed 12×12 table, with bonds between different letters. The reduction is from Hamiltonian path. The appendix proves the cube lemma, including the case of equality.
papers.why: A deterministic proof with a finite alphabet. It proves the cube lemma that Berger and Leighton cite without proof.

relations.note: Twelve letters instead of two, on the cubic lattice. Its appendix proves the cube lemma, which Berger and Leighton only cite.
Hart and Istrail asked for hardness with contact energies and a finite alphabet.

papers.title: Efficient algorithms for protein sequence design and the analysis of certain evolutionary fitness landscapes
papers.gist: The sequence-design problem of Sun et al. is solvable in polynomial time.
papers.why: Sequence design can be easy while folding is hard.

relations.note: Solves the Sun et al. design model in polynomial time, answering an open question of Hart.

papers.title: A Polynomial Time Upper Bound for the Number of Contacts in the HP-Model on the Face-Centered-Cubic Lattice (FCC)
papers.gist: An upper bound on the contacts of n H's on the face-centred cubic lattice, computed in polynomial time.
papers.takeaway: Backofen cuts the H's into layers that are square grids, bounds the contacts inside each layer and between neighbouring layers, and combines the bounds by dynamic programming in time of order n⁵. The bound is proved for sets whose layers have no gaps along a row or column. For 300 H's it allows 1461 contacts.
papers.why: On the cubic lattice the cube lemma gives the exact maximum, and Berger and Leighton build on it. On the face-centred cubic lattice this computed bound is what takes its place. The paper proves no hardness.

relations.note: The same model on the face-centred cubic lattice. It bounds contacts to speed up exact search and proves no hardness.

papers.title: Fast, Constraint-Based Threading of HP-Sequences to Hydrophobic Cores
papers.gist: Threads a given string onto a given compact set of nodes by constraint search.
papers.takeaway: The string must become a self-avoiding walk with every H on the given set. On random strings the search succeeds quickly for small sets; for a set of 100 nodes, half or more fail within the time limit.
papers.why: The second step of exact folding. On the cubic lattice, with the cube as the given set, this step is exactly the problem Berger and Leighton prove NP-hard (our observation; the paper does not say so).

relations.note: Threads strings onto the compact sets computed there.
Cites it for hardness. With the cube as the given set, its threading problem is the one Berger and Leighton prove hard.

papers.title: Optimally Compact Finite Sphere Packings — Hydrophobic Cores in the FCC
papers.gist: Computes the most compact sets of up to 100 nodes of the face-centred cubic lattice.
papers.takeaway: A search guided by layer bounds finds the sets of n nodes with the most neighbouring pairs, for example 436 pairs for 100 nodes. Optimal sets are not unique: there are two for 60 nodes and three for 100.
papers.why: The H's of a best fold form such a compact set, if the string allows it. On the cubic lattice the most compact set of n³ nodes is the cube, the target of Berger and Leighton's proof. Here the optimal sets are computed one size at a time, and their shapes vary.

relations.note: Cites it for hardness, and computes the counterpart of its cube on the face-centred cubic lattice.
Uses layer bounds of the same kind to prune the search.

papers.title: Constraint-Based Hydrophobic Core Construction for Protein Structure Prediction in the Face-Centered-Cubic Lattice
papers.gist: Lists all the most compact gap-free sets of H's on the face-centred cubic lattice, up to about 100.
papers.takeaway: A constraint program, pruned by layer bounds, builds every optimal set that has no gap along a lattice line. Threading strings through these sets gives optimal folds in practice: 60% of random strings of length 160 with 100 H's were solved within 15 minutes.
papers.why: Shows how far exact search reaches on this lattice. The method has no polynomial time bound, and the paper claims no complexity result.

relations.note: Takes its bounds for each sequence of layers from this paper.
Cites it for the first contact bounds on this lattice.

papers.title: Long proteins with unique optimal foldings in the H-P model
papers.gist: 2D HP strings of every length divisible by 4 whose optimal fold is unique.
papers.takeaway: Whether folding stays NP-hard for such strings is open.
papers.why: These are rigid gadgets in the HP model itself. The known hardness proofs produce many optimal folds, so they do not cover such strings.

relations.note: Requiring a unique optimal fold defeats the known hardness proofs.
Requiring a unique optimal fold defeats the known hardness proofs.

papers.title: The algorithmics of folding proteins on lattices
papers.gist: A 2003 survey of algorithms for folding on lattices.
papers.takeaway: It calls the hardness proofs involved and sketches the construction of Berger and Leighton. The proof that a perfect fold gives a packing is left out, and the 2D proof is only named.
papers.why: A second survey that restates the 3D proof without simplifying it.

relations.note: Sketches the construction and leaves out the proof that a perfect fold gives a packing.

papers.title: The inverse protein folding problem on 2D and 3D lattices
papers.gist: Canonical inverse folding is polynomial in 2D and NP-complete in 3D.
papers.takeaway: Hart's 2D reduction is wrong. The 3D problem has a PTAS.
papers.why: It corrects a published proof, and gives a problem whose 2D and 3D versions differ in complexity.

relations.note: The 2D reduction is not correct. 2D canonical inverse folding is solvable in O(K|V|) time.

papers.title: A Constraint-Based Approach to Fast and Exact Structure Prediction in Three-Dimensional Protein Models
papers.gist: Proves folds optimal on the cubic and face-centred cubic lattices, on the latter for 200 letters.
papers.takeaway: Compact sets for the H's are computed once and stored. A string is tried on the sets with the most contacts first, then on sets with one contact fewer, and so on; the first set it fits on gives an optimal fold. The paper also counts all optimal folds of some cubic-lattice strings exactly.
papers.why: The main evidence of how far exact computation reaches on the face-centred cubic lattice, where no hardness proof is known. Its starting point, that a best fold packs the H's tightly, is also where Berger and Leighton's cube comes from.

relations.note: Journal account of the construction of compact sets, with bounds for the cubic lattice added.
Journal account of the threading, with the fallback to less compact sets added.
Cited for hardness of HP folding.

papers.title: Geometric Folding Algorithms: Linkages, Origami, Polyhedra
papers.gist: The standard book on folding algorithms. Section 9.3 covers the HP model.
papers.takeaway: We have not seen the text.
papers.why: The book version of Demaine's lectures. We do not know whether it sketches either proof.

papers.title: Jigsaw Puzzles, Edge Matching, and Polyomino Packing: Connections and Complexity
papers.gist: Packing polyominoes is NP-complete, and equivalent to jigsaw and edge-matching puzzles.
papers.why: Packing polyominoes is close to placing items in bins.

papers.title: CPSP-tools – Exact and Complete Algorithms for High-Throughput 3D Lattice Protein Studies
papers.gist: Software that finds and counts optimal folds and designs strings on 3D lattices.
papers.takeaway: The tools reuse a stored database of compact sets of H's. They return every optimal fold, count them, and design strings with a unique optimal fold. All worked examples are strings of 27 letters on the cubic lattice.
papers.why: A ready tool for checking small instances on the cubic and face-centred cubic lattices. It proves nothing new about complexity.

relations.note: Implements its method.
Cited for hardness of string design in 3D and its ease in 2D.

papers.title: Fitting protein chains to cubic lattice is NP-complete
papers.gist: Fitting a given off-lattice chain to the cubic lattice as closely as possible is NP-complete.
papers.takeaway: Closeness is measured by the root-mean-square deviation of the coordinates.
papers.why: A related lattice problem with a given chain and no HP energy.

papers.title: Not being (super)thin or solid is hard: A study of grid Hamiltonicity
papers.gist: Maps which classes of square, triangular and hexagonal grid graphs have a hard Hamiltonian cycle.
papers.why: Relevant if a reduction targets a lattice other than the square one.

papers.title: Combinatorial Algorithms for Protein Folding in Lattice Models: A Survey of Mathematical Results
papers.gist: The standard survey of the mathematics of lattice HP models.
papers.takeaway: It restates both hardness theorems without proofs and lists hardness on the hexagonal lattice as open. Its Theorem 3.7 states the 2D parity bound without the term for H's at the ends of the string; that form fails for HPPHPHPH (our check).
papers.why: It describes both proofs as involved and gives no simpler one. Its list of hardness results ends in 1999.

relations.note: Theorem 4.10: the 3D result, from bin packing, with the cube lemma.
Theorem 4.9: the 2D result, which the survey describes as a reduction from Hamiltonian cycle with Trevisan codes.
Approximation algorithms and the parity bound (Theorems 3.6–3.8). Theorem 3.7 drops the term for H's at the ends of the string.
Listed among the hardness theorems (Theorem 4.1).
Listed among the hardness theorems (Theorem 4.2).
Listed among the hardness theorems (Theorem 4.3).
Listed among the hardness theorems.
Listed among the hardness theorems (Theorem 4.5).
Listed among the hardness theorems.
Listed among the hardness theorems (Theorem 4.8).

papers.title: Equivalence Classes of Optimal Structures in HP Protein Models Including Side Chains
papers.gist: Counts optimal folds up to the positions of the H's, which removes most duplicates.
papers.takeaway: Two optimal folds count as one if every H sits in the same place. For random 27-letter strings on the cubic lattice, the average drops from about 125,000 optimal folds to about 4,900 classes.
papers.why: Most optimal folds of an HP string differ only in where the P's go. Background for the question of strings with a unique optimal fold.

relations.note: Adds a tool to the package that lists one fold per class.
Both concern how many optimal folds a string has; we relate them, the paper does not cite it.

papers.title: Upper Bounds for Foldings in the FCC-HP Protein Model
papers.gist: Sharpens the face-centred cubic contact bound by cutting the H's into triangular layers.
papers.takeaway: In a triangular layer each node has six neighbours in its layer and three in each adjacent one. The dynamic program runs in time of order n⁴ and lowers the earlier bound by at most two contacts, for example from 438 to 436 for 100 H's. Most of the case analysis is left out of the paper.
papers.why: A slightly sharper answer to how many contacts n H's can make on this lattice. It proves no hardness.

relations.note: The same method with triangular layers instead of square ones.

papers.title: Optimal Binary Space Partitions for Segments in the Plane
papers.gist: The usual citation for planar monotone rectilinear 3SAT.
papers.takeaway: We have not checked the attribution.
papers.why: This form of 3SAT has a layout that suits gadgets on a grid.

papers.title: 6.849 Geometric Folding Algorithms: Linkages, Origami, Polyhedra (Fall 2012). Lecture 21: HP Model & Interlocked Chains; Class 20: 3D Linkage Folding
papers.gist: MIT lectures on folding that pose a simpler hardness proof as an open problem.
papers.takeaway: Demaine skips both hardness proofs as complicated. His open problems are a simpler or cleaner proof, APX-hardness, and a (1+ε)-approximation.
papers.why: States the open problem this project takes up.

relations.note: Summarizes the 3D reduction from bin packing and asks for a simpler proof.
Summarizes the 2D reduction from Hamiltonicity and asks for a simpler proof.

papers.title: Finding a Hamiltonian Path in a Cube with Specified Turns is Hard
papers.gist: Filling a cube with a chain whose turns are prescribed is NP-hard.
papers.takeaway: With every residue an H, this gives NP-hardness of fixed-angle HP folding in 3D.
papers.why: The target is Berger and Leighton's perfect cube, with every turn given.

relations.note: Fill the n×n×n cube with a chain whose turns are given. With every residue an H, this is fixed-angle HP folding.

papers.statusNote: We know it through Demaine et al. (2022).

papers.title: Is Protein Folding Problem Really a NP-Complete One? First Investigations
papers.gist: A modelling critique of the 2D proof. It claims no mathematical error.
papers.takeaway: The proof ranges over all self-avoiding walks. Pivot moves from the straight chain reach only some of them.
papers.why: A reminder to state the set of folds exactly: all self-avoiding walks on the lattice.

relations.note: The proof ranges over all self-avoiding walks, including folds that pivot moves from the straight chain cannot reach. Correctness is not disputed.

papers.title: Calculation of the connective constant for self-avoiding walks via the pivot algorithm
papers.gist: Estimates how fast the number of self-avoiding walks on the cubic lattice grows: about 4.684 per step.
papers.takeaway: The estimate comes from simulations with the pivot algorithm, which samples very long walks. It is a numerical value, not a theorem; no exact value is known.
papers.why: Every fold of a string is a self-avoiding walk, so a string with n+1 letters has roughly 4.68 to the power n folds on the cubic lattice. Trying them all is hopeless, but that alone does not make folding hard.

papers.title: Hamiltonicity is Hard in Thin or Polygonal Grid Graphs, but Easy in Thin Polygonal Grid Graphs
papers.gist: Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete in polygonal square grid graphs and thin hexagonal grid graphs.
papers.takeaway: These are two cases that Arkin et al. left open.
papers.why: Thin grid graphs stay hard. They might correspond to narrow forced corridors in a fold (our idea).

relations.note: Settles two cases that Arkin et al. left open.

papers.title: Polynomial-Time Reductions in Isabelle/HOL (poly-reductions)
papers.gist: An unfinished Isabelle catalogue of Karp reductions.
papers.takeaway: SAT to independent set, vertex cover and set cover, and vertex cover to Hamiltonian cycle. No longer active.
papers.why: Earlier work on formal reductions in Isabelle.

papers.title: Mechanising Complexity Theory: The Cook-Levin Theorem in Coq
papers.gist: The Cook–Levin theorem in Coq.
papers.takeaway: Running time is measured in a lambda calculus, with certified extraction from Coq functions.
papers.why: Time is measured in a functional model instead of on Turing machines.

papers.title: Emergence of Wulff-Crystals from Atomistic Systems on the FCC and HCP Lattices
papers.gist: On the face-centred cubic lattice, the densest large sets of nodes approach a truncated octahedron.
papers.takeaway: For N nodes the number of missing pairs grows like N to the power 2/3, and the rescaled optimal sets converge to the Wulff shape of an explicit surface energy. The paper also treats the hexagonal close-packed lattice.
papers.why: The face-centred cubic counterpart of the cube lemma, but only in the limit and up to lower-order terms. The paper has no strings and says nothing about complexity.

papers.title: Computational Complexity of Flattening Fixed-Angle Orthogonal Chains
papers.gist: Fixed-angle HP folding is strongly NP-complete in 2D, even with only two H's.
papers.takeaway: In 3D the fixed-angle case follows from Abel et al. together with the cube lemma.
papers.why: Fixing the angles makes hardness easy. In the original proofs every angle is free.

relations.note: Fixed-angle HP chains on the square grid, strongly NP-complete even with two H's.
The 3D fixed-angle case follows from Abel et al. together with the cube lemma.

papers.title: Bicolored Path Embedding Problems Inspired by Protein Folding Models
papers.gist: Folding a two-coloured path into a given grid graph with the most contacts is NP-hard.
papers.takeaway: The reductions, from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs, take about three pages, because the region to fill is part of the input.
papers.why: The reduction is short once the region is given. Forcing the region with the H/P energy alone is the hard part.

relations.note: Short reductions from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs.
The host region is part of the input. Their introduction contrasts this with the Hadamard-code proof.

papers.title: The Cook-Levin theorem
papers.gist: The Cook–Levin theorem in Isabelle, with running-time proofs for multi-tape Turing machines.
papers.why: Shows what running-time proofs at the level of Turing machines cost.

papers.title: Verification of NP-hardness Reduction Functions for Exact Lattice Problems
papers.gist: Isabelle proofs that NP-hardness reductions for two lattice problems are correct.
papers.takeaway: The problems are the closest and the shortest vector problem. Running time is argued on paper. The formalization found and fixed problems in the published proofs.
papers.why: A precedent for proving the correctness of a reduction formally and arguing its running time in prose.

relations.note: Its Isabelle entry takes its definition of reductions from poly-reductions (from a search result; we have not opened the entry).

papers.title: Ptyche: Dill's hydrophobic-polar protein folding model in Lean 4
papers.gist: The HP model in Lean 4: folds, the contact score and score bounds.
papers.takeaway: It also has a verified search for optimal folds. It is the only formalization of the model we found, and it has no hardness results.
papers.why: A possible base for Lean definitions of the model.

relations.note: Folds, contact score and score bounds of Dill's HP model in Lean 4. No NP-hardness.
A Lean 4 library built on Mathlib.

papers.title: ASP-Completeness of Hamiltonicity in Grid Graphs, with Applications to Loop Puzzles
papers.gist: Hamiltonicity in grid graphs of maximum degree 3 is ASP-complete.
papers.takeaway: The introduction maps the known hardness results for Hamiltonicity.
papers.why: Its reductions are parsimonious, which could give #P-hardness of counting optimal folds (our idea).

relations.note: Adds the cycle version for maximum degree 3, and ASP-completeness.
Its introduction maps the hardness results for Hamiltonicity.

papers.title: CSLib: the Lean computer science library (Computability, Turing machines, TimeM)
papers.gist: The official Lean library for computer science. It has no NP.
papers.takeaway: It has polynomial-time Turing machines. Its cost monad counts steps by annotations that Lean does not check.
papers.why: Costs that are annotations cannot back a claim of verified running time.

relations.note: A complexity library built on Mathlib.

papers.title: cslib-frontier: frontier formalization library for CSLib (formerly Complexitylib)
papers.gist: Polynomial-time reductions in Lean, with about 40 problems proved NP-complete.
papers.takeaway: It has a tactic for proofs of polynomial running time. The build is heavy.
papers.why: The most usable Lean framework for polynomial-time reductions we found. It is large, written with AI assistance, and not ours.

relations.note: Adds NP, reductions and NP-completeness on top of CSLib.
Depends on Mathlib.

papers.title: Mathlib4: Computability (TM2, encodings, reductions) and SimpleGraph
papers.gist: Lean's main library has polynomial-time Turing machines, but no NP.
papers.takeaway: It has no polynomial-time reductions. The grid ℤ² can be built as a product of graphs.
papers.why: This is what Lean work can build on without other libraries.

papers.title: NP-completeness of SAT and its variants: the Cook–Levin theorem in Lean 4
papers.gist: Turing machines in core Lean, with SAT and planar 3SAT proved NP-complete.
papers.why: It was written by AI and, according to its README, has not been reviewed by a person.

relations.note: Proves planar 3SAT, including Lichtenstein's version, NP-complete in Lean.

papers.title: Descriptive Complexity in Lean: Completeness by First-Order Reductions
papers.gist: NP-completeness in Lean through logic, for Cook–Levin and all 21 of Karp's problems.
papers.takeaway: NP is defined logically. Hardness is shown by first-order reductions, which are automatically polynomial-time.
papers.why: NP-completeness without machines or running-time proofs.

relations.note: Built on Mathlib's model theory.

papers.title: lean-np-hardness: NP-hardness foundations in Lean
papers.gist: P, NP and reductions on Mathlib's Turing machines, with SAT and MaxCut NP-complete.
papers.takeaway: About 54,000 lines, built with AI.
papers.why: A measure of what NP-hardness on Mathlib's Turing machines costs.

relations.note: Builds P, NP and reductions on Mathlib's TM2 machines.
